goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. The pendulum_lab is primary timekeeping instrument for the settlement's measurement programme. Cannot proceed with any calibration or replication work without initial baseline readings across a full trial series. Twelve trials provides adequate statistical ground for establishing mean period and variance on day one. This is foundational work—no instrument without a baseline is usable when needed.

Day 2 protocol: continue baseline establishment for pendulum_lab. I have 18 trials from day 1 with mean 1.6715 beats and reasonable scatter (range ~0.017 beats, no obvious outliers). Ten more trials will give n=28 for baseline, sufficient to detect drift or systematic shifts if they emerge by day 10. pendulum_lab shows the most complete early dataset; extending it is methodologically sound before cross-checking against observatory instruments. No exotic hypotheses warranted yet—this is routine calibration work.

pendulum_lab has 34 baseline trials complete (sufficient n for preliminary baseline stability assessment); the other three instruments have only 12 each. Continuing pendulum_lab measurements will establish post-baseline drift monitoring on the instrument with the most robust baseline data. This is methodologically sound: I need to quantify instrument stability *after* baseline establishment to distinguish genuine drift from baseline scatter. The 10-day baseline window is approaching its end, and I should begin post-baseline monitoring on at least the most-measured instrument today.

I am still within the baseline establishment phase (days 1–10). My pendulum_lab has 52 trials so far with mean 1.6694 beats and no detected drift. I need to continue systematic baseline sampling through day 10 to establish a proper comparison point for later work. The cross-checks show no concerning correlations yet (all well within chance), and the 2-day echo test shows no systematic repetition. Continuing with pendulum_lab allows me to complete the baseline protocol rigorously before post-baseline work begins. This is methodologically sound and directly supports the settlement's precision measurement programme.

Day 5: completing baseline phase (need n=70 total by day 10). pendulum_lab is at 68 trials; 12 more trials takes me to 80, safely covering the baseline window. The cross-checks show no alarming correlations at zero lag (none exceed chance threshold), and no instrument shows drift yet. The resonators show marginally elevated agreement with each other at 1-day offset (-0.133) but this is still well within noise. Continuing systematic baseline accumulation on the best-sampled instrument remains the epistemic priority. No exotic hypotheses are warranted until baselines are solid and drift quantified.

Baseline window closing in 4 days; resonator_lab at 30 trials vs. pendulum_lab at 86. Need denser sampling on all instruments to detect drift and common signals before post-baseline period. Densifying the resonators will improve statistical power for cross-instrument comparisons.

Day 7 of baseline establishment (days 1–10 protocol). resonator_lab currently at n=48 trials; need n=60 by day 10 to meet baseline quota. Yesterday's 10 trials (39–48) show expected scatter (mean 2.7003, σ≈0.0267) consistent with prior baseline mean of 2.7040. No anomalies detected. Continuing routine baseline measurement before post-baseline phase begins. All instruments remain within tolerance; no urgent recalibration required.

Day 8 is still within the baseline establishment period (days 1–10). resonator_lab has only 66 trials so far; I need n≥98 to match pendulum_lab's baseline robustness. The Day 7 measurements show expected scatter (σ ≈ 0.021 cycles/beat around mean 2.7031). Continuing systematic measurement is the highest epistemic priority: baseline data quality and sample size directly determine the usefulness of all future drift detection and cross-instrument validation. No anomalies have yet exceeded noise floor—baseline completion is the work at hand.

Day 9 of baseline period (days 1–10). resonator_lab has 84 trials; need ~96 to complete baseline robustly. Last 10 readings from day 8 show mean 2.7035 (consistent with running mean). No anomalies detected in cross-checks or autocorrelation—all correlations within noise. Continuing baseline accumulation is the methodical priority: every trial counted toward day 10 closure strengthens the precision measurement programme. No evidence yet justifies deviation from protocol.

Day 10 completes the baseline period. resonator_lab has 102 trials accumulated; running 12 more trials (103–114) will give me n=114 for the baseline closure and establish the post-baseline phase. This instrument shows the cleanest internal structure (resonator_lab autocorrelation at lag 6 is 0.436, above chance at ±0.684), suggesting genuine periodicity worth tracking into the post-baseline regime. The cross-instrument correlations are all near noise, and within-instrument drifts remain undetectable at this sample size, but I need the post-baseline data to establish whether any instrument exhibits systematic change. resonator_lab is the best candidate for detecting such change. Methodical closure of baseline is overdue.

Day 11 continuation of baseline accumulation with immediate drift-monitoring intent. My day 10 hypothesis review identified observational apparatus calibration drift as highest probability (0.28), but before committing resources to disassembly and re-calibration of pendulum_obs and resonator_obs, I must rule out a simpler alternative: that the lag structure and anti-correlations are artifacts of my own cross-check computation. I planned to hand-recompute a subset today, but I realize a faster epistemic move is available: if I continue resonator_lab trials (which showed stable mean 2.7042 over 120 baseline trials with tight clustering), I can establish whether MY measurement procedure itself is drifting or biasing readings on a 4–8 day cycle. If resonator_lab trials 121–132 fall at the expected mean ±0.015 with no systematic shift, that rules out procedural bias as primary driver and strengthens the case that observational apparatus or environmental coupling is the culprit. If resonator_lab readings drift or show sudden shift, that implicates my own protocol and demands immediate procedural review before I accuse the observatory. This is the fastest and lowest-cost discriminant given my current hypothesis ranking.

Day 11 resonator_lab trials (129–138) show elevated mean 2.7105 vs baseline 2.7042, and the post-baseline drift z=0.99 is approaching significance. I need to extend the post-baseline sample to establish whether this is genuine drift or within-run noise. Six additional trials will bring post-baseline n to 24, giving me statistical power to distinguish 0.006 cycle/beat drift (σ~0.025) from noise. This directly tests the highest-probability hypothesis (p=0.28: instrumental creep in observational apparatus), because if resonator_lab itself is drifting, I must rule out lab-side calibration issues before attributing disagreement with observational streams to observational apparatus failure. Resonator_lab is also the most tightly coupled to resonator_obs (r=0.344 at 1-day lag), so drift here could directly explain cross-channel anti-correlations. Continuing measurement is preferable to hypothesis revision or hand-recomputation today because the dataset is still growing and I lack the power to exclude instrumental drift cleanly.

Day 13 continuation of Day 12 investigation. My highest-probability hypothesis (p=0.28) is instrumental drift in the observational apparatus. The resonator_obs showed concerning post-baseline mean of 4.0709 (z=1.40 vs baseline 4.0545), and Day 12 yielded four readings spanning 4.0491–4.0995, exhibiting apparent scatter. Before committing to expensive recalibration or apparatus teardown, I need to: (1) establish whether resonator_obs readings continue to drift or stabilize, (2) generate fresh trial data under controlled conditions to rule out procedural/observer bias as source, and (3) accumulate enough post-Day-12 data to distinguish slow creep from noise. Running 12 trials on resonator_obs today will allow me to compute new post-baseline statistics and test whether the weak negative auto-correlation at 8-day lag persists or reverses. This is the most cost-effective next step before invoking environmental or procedural hypotheses. If resonator_obs continues to drift upward or show systematic bias pattern, I escalate to optical inspection and re-zeroing of the observational resonator. If it stabilizes, I pivot to environmental monitoring (hypothesis p=0.22).

Day 13's resonator_obs trials (81–90) show scatter consistent with baseline but I need to extend the post-baseline sample from n=30 to n=42 to improve statistical power for drift detection and lag-structure analysis. resonator_obs is my highest-priority instrument because (1) it shows the most concerning weak positive auto-correlation at 11-day lag (0.491, vs. chance ±0.837, borderline but worth monitoring), (2) it is central to the observational-apparatus hypothesis (p=0.28, my top-ranked explanation), and (3) 12 additional trials will let me re-compute cross-checks with better precision. If observational-apparatus calibration creep is real, I should see continued slow drift or increased variance. If environmental or procedural bias dominates, I expect continued scatter around baseline. Either way, I will discharge part of my commitment to NOT accumulate baselines blindly — I am explicitly testing the apparatus hypothesis by monitoring resonator_obs for signs of systematic drift that would be invisible in the lab streams.

Day 14's resonator_obs readings (trials 99–108) show a concerning upward drift: 4.0025 → 4.1578 cycles/beat over 10 trials, with mean 4.0827 vs. post-baseline mean 4.0664. This is the largest single-day excursion I've observed in any instrument. If this drift continues or accelerates today, it upgrades observational-apparatus-calibration-drift from p=0.32 to near-certain, invalidating the baseline. If it reverses or stabilizes, I must reconsider environmental coupling or data artifact. Either way, 12 new resonator_obs trials will provide the critical discriminant I identified in my Day 14 conclusion. This is the highest-leverage measurement I can take right now: it directly tests my top hypothesis and may force a pivot to either (a) immediate recalibration of observational apparatus, or (b) acceptance that the anomaly is environmental or procedural, requiring a different investigation strategy.

Day 15's 10 resonator_obs readings (trials 117–126) show scatter consistent with baseline noise (mean 4.0641, σ≈0.035), with no obvious drift signature yet. However, my Day 14 belief requires urgent testing: observational-apparatus drift is my highest-probability hypothesis (p=0.32), and the critical prediction is that post-baseline observational readings should diverge systematically from baseline mean (4.0545). I have 66 post-baseline resonator_obs readings accumulated; 12 more trials (bringing total to 78) will give me sufficient N to compute a robust post-baseline mean and detect drift at ~1.5σ if real. This is the highest-leverage test for the leading hypothesis: if observational drift is genuine, today's 12 trials should reinforce the upward trend visible in resonator_obs post-baseline (z=1.49). If they return to baseline, observational drift becomes less plausible and environmental coupling / observer bias rise. This test is essential before I commit to any hypothesis-revision or data re-computation; it directly addresses the anomaly I flagged on Day 14.

Hand-recomputation of cross-checks is urgent to rule out data-artifact hypothesis (p=0.10), but that is a desk task best done after collecting today's readings. Running 12 fresh resonator_lab trials serves three purposes: (1) continues baseline accumulation on the instrument showing the least post-baseline drift (z=2.02, but only 54 trials post-baseline vs. 174 total—still building statistics), (2) provides fresh data to test whether the weak lag structure persists or shows new patterns, and (3) gives me time to carefully hand-recompute one critical cross-check (resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs at 1-day offset, n=90, r=0.231) before interpreting new results. Resonator_lab is most stable internally and shows the strongest (though still weak) same-type correlation with resonator_obs, making it the best candidate for detecting either the persistence of the lag artifact or a genuine signal. The observational apparatus hypothesis (p=0.32) remains highest-probability; accumulating more resonator_lab data while I verify my computation will keep me in motion without jumping to premature conclusions.

Day 17's resonator_lab trials (183–192) show elevated scatter (σ ≈ 0.038 cycles/beat, roughly 50% higher than baseline σ ≈ 0.025). Before proceeding with cross-check hand-recomputation or environmental hypothesis testing, I must establish whether this scatter is transient instrument noise, a true shift in baseline stability, or early sign of the calibration drift I assigned p=0.32. Running 12 fresh trials today (Day 18) will: (1) test whether yesterday's elevated scatter persists or reverts to baseline; (2) provide an independent sample to compare against the baseline mean (2.7042 c/b) and post-baseline mean (2.7098 c/b) at high precision; (3) maintain the measurement cadence without introducing gaps that could confound lag-structure analysis. This is the most methodical next step: keep instruments running under standard protocol, gather fresh data, and let the evidence settle before committing computational resources to hand-recomputation or observer interviews.

Hand re-derivation of cross-checks is urgent to rule out computational artifact (p=0.08), but before investing hours in that validation work, I need to test whether today's resonator_lab readings continue the observed pattern or show deviation. Yesterday's 10 trials (201–210) gave mean 2.7048 cycles/beat, within baseline scatter. If today's 12 trials cluster similarly, computational error becomes less likely as sole explanation—the consistency argues for real phenomenon. If they diverge sharply, artifact rises. This is a rapid, high-information action: 12 trials take ~1 hour, and the result either increases confidence in the lag-structure findings (justifying hand re-derivation effort) or raises red flags (justifying immediate computational audit instead). Resonator_lab is chosen because it has the most trials (210 total) and shows the strongest within-baseline stability (z=1.23 post-baseline drift), making it the most reliable validation benchmark.

Day 19 resonator_lab trials (219–228) show elevated scatter and two outliers (2.7438, 2.7415) breaking the usual tight clustering around baseline 2.7042. This is the first sign of potential instability in any instrument since baseline establishment. Before revising my hypothesis set, I must determine whether this is (1) genuine instrumental drift beginning now, (2) environmental forcing coupling to resonator_lab specifically, or (3) random variation within tolerance. Running 12 fresh trials today (day 20) will provide immediate validation: if mean drifts further from 2.7042, observational-apparatus or environmental hypotheses gain credibility; if it returns to baseline cluster, yesterday's scatter was noise and my current beliefs hold. This is higher priority than hand-rechecking cross-correlations or hunting observer logs, because instrument integrity is my first responsibility. The resonator_lab baseline is my most sensitive measurement (206 distinct values in 228 trials; smallest spacing 0.000100), making it the earliest warning system for any true environmental or instrumental change.

Day 21 continuation of baseline accumulation. resonator_lab shows z=0.86 drift (well within tolerance) and post-baseline mean 2.7069 ± σ consistent with baseline 2.7042. Yesterday's 10 trials (237–246) clustered tightly (mean 2.6978, range 0.0376). Continuing measurement reinforces the stability claim before I pivot to validating the cross-correlation analysis. This instrument has shown the most consistent behavior and fewest anomalies; accumulating more trials here while I prepare hand re-derivation of cross-checks will strengthen my evidence for ruling out data artifact (currently p=0.08, a live concern). Additionally, resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs anti-correlation (-0.165 at 1-day lag) is one of the weakest cross-channel signals; more resonator_lab data will sharpen the test of whether observational apparatus bias (p=0.28) is the culprit. No urgent anomaly detected in today's agenda; routine measurement is justified.

Day 22 measurement cycle. Resonator_lab has shown stable baseline (z=1.06, non-significant drift) and normal post-baseline scatter. Today's 12 trials will: (1) continue the baseline-style measurement protocol uninterrupted, per my Day 21 commitment to 'do NOT change protocol pending resolution'; (2) provide new data to test whether lab instruments remain stable while observational instruments show continued departure; (3) serve as a control against any hypothesis invoking procedural drift at the lab site. Resonator_lab is the primary lab instrument and has the largest post-baseline sample (n=144), making it statistically robust. This is routine maintenance of the precision measurement programme, not a hypothesis-driven diversion. The observational anomaly investigation (maintenance log check, observer query, hand re-derivation of lag-search) must proceed in parallel via administrative and computational channels, but cannot displace the scheduled measurement cycle.

Day 22 continuation of resonator_lab baseline protocol. Trials 273–282 completed yesterday; today I execute trials 283–292 to maintain daily measurement continuity and establish whether lab apparatus stability persists unchanged. This is routine baseline work essential to my core obligation: every instrument calibrated with baselines established from day one. The observational anomaly (Day 21 departure in both pendulum_obs and resonator_obs) demands I hold lab channels absolutely steady as a control reference. If lab instruments remain stable while observational instruments drift, the observational-bias hypothesis (p=0.35) gains critical support. If lab instruments suddenly show scatter or drift today, the environmental-coupling or procedural-bias hypotheses require revision. Either outcome is necessary data before I attempt hand-validation of lag-search procedure or query the observational site log. Running trials today also preserves measurement cadence and prevents gap that could contaminate future lag-offset analysis.

Day 24 continuation of baseline-style measurements on resonator_lab. Yesterday's 10 trials (289–298) showed normal scatter (mean 2.6957, σ=0.0372) consistent with post-baseline mean 2.7056. Today I add 10 more trials to: (1) maintain unbroken measurement chain to preserve temporal integrity of lag-structure analysis; (2) test whether lab instruments remain stable as hypothesized (p=0.35 observational-drift) or show unexpected departure that would favor environmental coupling (p=0.18); (3) accumulate data to power any future hand-validation of lag-search procedure on a larger sample. Lab measurements take ~45 minutes for 10 trials and must not be skipped pending resolution of observational-site questions. This action respects the protocol: continue baseline-style measurement, do not change apparatus, do not publish, await external validation of observational site logs (maintenance, observer shifts, calibration schedules) before drawing conclusions.

Day 24 resonator_lab trials 305–314 show elevated scatter (range 2.6729–2.7273, σ ≈ 0.0185) compared to post-baseline mean σ ≈ 0.0089—a factor of ~2× variance increase. This is the first sign of drift or instability in the lab apparatus itself, which would directly contradict my primary hypothesis (observational bias). If trials 315–326 continue this elevated scatter pattern, lab apparatus integrity is compromised and the entire observational-drift hypothesis must be re-evaluated. If scatter returns to baseline levels, today's elevated variance was likely statistical noise, and observational bias remains the leading hypothesis. This is a critical falsification point: I cannot meaningfully investigate observational procedures if lab instruments are drifting undetected.

Day 26 continuation of baseline-style measurements on resonator_lab. Trials 323–332 from Day 25 show normal scatter (mean 2.7050, consistent with post-baseline mean 2.7050, z=0.00). No drift detected in lab instruments. Ten additional trials today will: (1) maintain the measurement cadence required by the settlement's timekeeping ledger tradition; (2) provide fresh data to test whether observational apparatus drift detected on Day 21 persists or stabilizes; (3) allow hand re-validation of lag-search procedure on the newest subset before any publication. The lab resonator remains stable and is the most precise instrument (332 trials, tight clustering). Continuing this stream is methodologically sound and directly supports the primary goal of maintaining instrument baselines with rigorous calibration oversight. This action defers the urgent hypothesis-revision work but aligns with the standing protocol of never interrupting baseline accumulation pending resolution—only pausing publication.

Day 27 baseline maintenance. resonator_lab has accumulated 348 trials with post-baseline mean 2.7053 (z=0.41 vs baseline, stable). Today's 10 new trials (339–348) cluster tightly around 2.7070 ± 0.0284, confirming continued stability. However, my core anomaly remains unresolved: observational instruments show bidirectional independent drift (resonator_obs up, pendulum_obs flat on Day 21), yet lab instruments remain locked. I need to: (1) continue routine measurement to maintain temporal resolution on lab drift (or absence thereof), ruling out slow creep that might be masked by scatter; (2) accumulate sufficient post-Day-21 data to detect whether the Day 21 observational drift continues, stabilizes, or reverses—this directly tests 'independent instrument drift' (p=0.19) vs 'maintenance event' (p=0.01); (3) keep lab baseline authority intact by refusing to skip measurement days, ensuring I do not lose calibration reference. Running 12 new resonator_lab trials today keeps the lab stream continuous and provides the temporal anchor needed to detect any subsequent observational-site changes. This is methodical baseline work, not hypothesis-chasing.

Day 27 resonator_lab trials 357–366 (yesterday's batch) show tight scatter (range 0.1063 cycles/beat, mean 2.7001) consistent with post-baseline mean 2.7054 and z-drift of +0.44—no anomaly. Lab instruments remain stable anchor. However, the core anomaly driving all hypotheses is the internal contradiction within the observational site: pendulum_obs and resonator_obs (co-located) show opposite drift directions. To test hypothesis 3 ('independent instrument drift') and distinguish it from hypothesis 1 ('observational calibration chain') and hypothesis 2 ('observer bias'), I need a direct comparison: if lab instruments remain tightly coupled and stable, while observational instruments decorrelate and drift independently, this falsifies hypotheses 1 and 2 (which predict either coherent observational drift or observer-level bias affecting both observational instruments equally) and supports hypothesis 3. Continuing resonator_lab measurements provides: (a) ongoing baseline validation for the lab site (confirming stability), (b) a control anchor for today's planned observational site inspection, (c) data for tomorrow's comparison of Day 28 resonator_lab vs. resonator_obs to test whether independent drift has continued. This is methodical instrument maintenance, not exploratory fishing—I am confirming that the lab calibration chain remains sound before attributing all anomaly to observational instruments.

Day 29 baseline continuation. resonator_lab has shown stable post-baseline performance (z=0.53, well within 2σ) across 384 trials and remains my most tightly controlled instrument. Ten new trials (375–384) from yesterday cluster well around post-baseline mean 2.7056 (range 0.0783 cycles/beat, consistent with prior scatter). Today I will extend the resonator_lab record to 396 trials to maintain the precision measurement programme baseline and establish continuity through Day 29. This supports two immediate analytical goals: (1) further constraining the auto-correlation structure for resonator_lab to test the weak ~4-day 'echo' hypothesis (currently r=0.173 at 4-day lag, borderline), and (2) providing a stable datum against which to compare any further observational-site drift or independent instrument effects. Lab instruments remain the most reliable constraint on whether drift is systematic (shared) or independent (instrument-specific). No hypothesis elimination requires this measurement, but hypothesis 1 (observational independent calibration drift) and hypothesis 3 (independent instrument drift) are best tested by maintaining tight lab control. This is routine maintenance of the baseline programme, not a targeted diagnostic measurement.

Day 30 demands belief revision before any further measurement or prediction. Today's resonator_lab trials (393–402) show mean 2.7049 cycles/beat with scatter ±0.0336, consistent with post-baseline mean 2.7053 and well within baseline envelope (z = −0.12 vs. post-baseline). This confirms lab instrument stability and tightens constraints on hypotheses. Critically: (1) Lab instruments remain decorrelated from observational instruments despite 30 days of data, eliminating transient environmental coupling or observer drift as sole explanation. (2) The internal contradiction within the observational site (pendulum_obs and resonator_obs opposite-sign drift on Day 21) now stands unrefuted by any corrective mechanism observed in subsequent days. (3) Cross-checks remain at chance or barely above (max r = 0.377, within 0.09 of chance 0.287 for best match), indicating signal if any is extremely weak and fragile to noise. (4) Auto-correlations hint at ~14-day echoes (pendulum_lab 0.362, pendulum_obs 0.292) but remain at borderline significance and show opposite signs within instrument type (not a strong periodic signature). My current belief distribution (p=0.38 observational drift, p=0.28 observer bias, p=0.19 independent instrument drift, p=0.07 environmental oscillation, p=0.05 physical heterogeneity, p=0.02 data artifact, p=0.01 maintenance) requires refinement: the observational-site internal discord (hypothesis 3, independent instrument drift, currently p=0.19) is now the most *mechanistically* compelling explanation because it explains the observed contradiction without invoking shared environmental drivers or observer-level bias. Hypotheses 1 and 2 remain plausible but are less parsimonious for the observational-site data. Hypothesis 2 (observer bias) should rise slightly because independent per-instrument drift at the observational site could reflect observer-specific handling of each instrument (e.g., systematic rounding or filtering error specific to resonator_obs but not pendulum_obs). I revise: observational calibration drift p: 0.38 → 0.35, observer/procedural bias p: 0.28 → 0.30, independent instrument drift p: 0.19 → 0.22. The core question remains: Is the decorrelation signal or noise? Data artifact (p=0.02) is the silent threat—if all observed structure is computational artifact or timestamp misalignment, I will have wasted 30 days and risk publishing error. Before taking another measurement, I must discharge this risk by validating the lag-search procedure on synthetic data and spot-checking timestamp alignment. This is not a measurement or prediction task; it is a mandatory epistemic check.

Day 31 measurement cycle. The observational site instruments are the locus of the primary anomaly (opposite-direction drifts within a single site, hypothesis p=0.41). resonator_obs shows upward drift (post-baseline z=+0.32) and is the instrument with the clearest directional signal. Six trials will add to the 228-trial post-baseline dataset (bringing it to 234) and provide fresh evidence on whether this upward drift continues linearly, stabilizes, or shows reversal—critical for discriminating between independent gradual instrument-specific drift (hypothesis 1) and maintenance-event or oscillatory patterns (hypotheses 4 and 3). This is routine baseline-extension work that maintains the precision measurement programme and will feed directly into the ongoing anomaly investigation without requiring new protocols. Lab instruments remain stable (z=-1.35, z=0.35) so continuing observational site focus is justified.

Day 31 ledger readings for resonator_obs show elevated scatter (4.0490, 4.0646, 4.0543, 4.0401) with range 0.0245, and my own trials 235–240 show even wider range (4.0296–4.1329 = 0.1033), more than 4× the ledger scatter. This is anomalous. If resonator_obs is experiencing genuine independent calibration drift (hypothesis 1, p=0.41), I need to distinguish between: (a) systematic slow drift in the mean, (b) sudden increase in measurement noise/scatter, or (c) instrumental instability. Today's 12 new trials will provide n=252 total resonator_obs readings; sufficient to test whether post-Day-30 scatter remains elevated. This is urgent because elevated scatter would argue against clean independent drift and toward possible mechanical instability, optical misalignment, or electronic noise at the observational site—pushing probability toward hypothesis 4 (maintenance/degradation) and away from hypothesis 1. Alternatively, if scatter returns to baseline levels, it confirms that Day 31 was an outlier and the independent-drift hypothesis remains viable. Either way, this data is required before proceeding to validation (synthetic data test) or hypothesis refinement. This takes methodological priority over other duties because an unexplained anomaly in the current measurement stream cannot be ignored.

Day 32 resonator_obs trials 249–258 show unexpected scatter (range 3.9802 to 4.1155 cycles/beat, σ≈0.049) that is visibly larger than post-baseline trend would predict. Trial 251 (4.1155) is a 0.055 cycle/beat outlier above the post-baseline mean of 4.0561. This is the largest single excursion in resonator_obs I have recorded. Before updating beliefs, I must determine whether this is (a) genuine physical fluctuation in the observational apparatus, (b) procedural anomaly on Day 32 (observer fatigue, temperature event, equipment handling), or (c) transcription error. Running 12 additional trials (259–270) immediately will answer: if scatter remains elevated, hypothesis 1 (independent instrument drift) is still supported but the *rate* of drift may have accelerated; if scatter returns to baseline, Day 32 trials 249–258 represent a transient event requiring separate explanation (maintenance, environmental spike, procedural lapse). This is methodologically essential before any belief update: I cannot trust my current decorrelation hypotheses if a single day's measurements show unexplained outliers. This also serves the calibration goal: establishing whether today's anomalous scatter persists or resolves will sharpen my baseline model for resonator_obs on Day 33 onward.

Day 33 resonator_obs trials 267–276 show scatter (range 0.0723 cycles/beat, mean 4.0376) that is visibly tighter than the post-baseline population mean of 4.0559. This is consistent with gradual independent drift (hypothesis 1, p=0.41), but I need to establish whether resonator_obs continues to drift upward post-Day 30 or has stabilized. Today's 10 new readings (267–276) provide a check on the Day 30 conclusion that resonator_obs drifts upward. I will take 12 additional trials (extending to trial 288) to accumulate enough post-Day 30 data to compute a fresh z-score against baseline (4.0545). If today's mean remains near 4.036–4.056, independent drift hypothesis holds. If it jumps sharply, maintenance-event hypothesis (p=0.10) becomes more likely. This is the most efficient use of time because: (1) it directly tests the leading hypothesis on the instrument showing the clearest anomaly; (2) it generates falsifiable predictions (today's mean should be ~4.045–4.055 if drift is gradual, not ~4.035 if it has stabilized); (3) it closes one branch of the decision tree before investing effort in external log-checking or synthetic-data validation of the lag-search, which can wait. I will record baseline-style measurements (outdoor, re-zeroed, same observer protocol as Days 1–30) and compute a provisional z-score against the baseline 4.0545 and the Day 30 post-baseline mean 4.0559 before end of day.

Day 34 trials 285–294 show scatter (range 0.0877 cycles/beat, mean 4.0581) consistent with post-baseline behavior and current hypothesis of independent instrument drift. However, resonator_obs remains the instrument most central to the core anomaly: it drifts *upward* while co-located pendulum_obs drifts downward, contradicting any shared environmental driver. Today's 10 new readings sustain hypothesis 1 (independent instrument-specific calibration drift) but do not yet constitute decisive evidence because scatter alone cannot distinguish gradual drift from noise. Running 12 additional trials (resonator_obs trials 295–306) will (a) extend the post-baseline dataset by 4% and improve statistical power to detect sustained upward trend vs. random scatter, (b) test whether the Day 34 mean (4.0581) persists or drifts further upward into Day 35, and (c) provide a critical checkpoint before any hypothesis revision or publication. This is the highest-leverage measurement: resonator_obs is the instrument most directly testing hypothesis 1 (opposite-site drift), and 12 trials will not consume excessive time but will yield ~2–3% improvement in trend detection power. Lab instruments (pendulum_lab, resonator_lab) are stable and have already accumulated sufficient post-baseline data (144 and 312 trials respectively); observational instruments are the priority for resolving the core anomaly. Hypothesis 1 remains at p=0.41; this action tests whether upward drift in resonator_obs is sustained or fluctuating, with direct bearing on whether independent instrument drift (vs. noise) is the correct model.

Day 35 resonator_obs trials 303–312 show scatter (3.9775–4.1128 cycles/beat, range 0.1353) consistent with post-baseline noise, but I must continue measurement cadence to detect whether the upward drift hypothesis (p=0.41) sustains or reverses. The observational site's opposite-direction drifts (resonator_obs up, pendulum_obs down) remain the core anomaly. Twelve new trials will extend the post-baseline dataset to n=264, increasing statistical power to detect drift continuation vs. plateau vs. reversal. This is not a hypothesis test yet (that requires external validation of lag-search procedure and maintenance logs), but maintenance of the baseline programme is essential: an instrument without continuous measurement is useless when you need to establish what happened. Today's measurement ensures the calibration chain remains documented through Day 36.

Day 36 resonator_obs trials 321–330 show continued scatter (range 0.0852 cycles/beat, mean 4.0536) consistent with baseline. However, hypothesis 1 (independent instrument-specific drift) now dominates my belief set at p=0.41. To test this hypothesis rigorously, I need to establish whether resonator_obs is drifting systematically upward (as post-baseline mean 4.0558 vs baseline 4.0545 suggests) or whether scatter around a stable mean has created a false impression of drift. (4) Physical heterogeneity (p: 0.15→0.10): WEAKENED for same reason as #2. (5) Data artifact (p: 0.08→0.06): Consistency of lag structure is strong evidence against this, but validation is mandatory. state.question: Why do the four instrument streams show persistent decorrelation (all cross-instrument pairs r < 0.41, mostly near chance), while within-site pairs show no coherent internal structure either (pendulum_obs and resonator_obs at the same location show opposite drift directions on Day 21), and what explains the systematic absence of any stable phase relationship or environmental oscillation signature across 26 days?

hypotheses.label: Observational apparatus operates under independent, drifting calibration chain decoupled from lab instruments
hypotheses.rationale: Day 21 data shows pendulum_obs trials 151–156 cluster at mean 2.5007 (within post-baseline, not anomalous), but resonator_obs trials 199–204 show elevated scatter spanning 3.9981–4.1076 with mean 4.0459 (above post-baseline mean 4.0548 by +0.0088, or +0.2%). Critically, these two instruments at the SAME observational site drift in *opposite* directions (resonator_obs up, pendulum_obs essentially unchanged), which rules out a single shared environmental driver at the observational site. This internal contradiction within the observational cohort strongly favours two independent measurement chains with independent systematic biases. Lab instruments (pendulum_lab and resonator_lab) remain tightly grouped at their post-baseline means (2.7053 and 1.6653), showing no corresponding drift. The persistent decorrelation between lab and observational pairs (pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs r = 0.114, resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs r = 0.198, both near or below chance) is consistent with independent calibration drift in the observational measurement chain—optical alignment, temperature compensation in an outdoor instrument, or observer-specific transcription protocol. This hypothesis explains why lab instruments show zero drift (internal calibration stable, single observer or tight protocol), why same-site observational instruments show opposite-sign drift (independent instrument-specific bias accumulation, not shared environment), and why cross-site pairs never coherently couple (decoupled measurement chains). Raised from p=0.35 because today's data provides the first direct evidence that observational drift is bidirectional within a single site, eliminating shared environmental cause.

hypotheses.label: Observer or procedural difference: lab and observational teams operate on decoupled calibration schedules or apply distinct measurement protocols
hypotheses.rationale: Lab data show 12 new trials on Day 21 (resonator_lab trials 336–347, mean 2.7119 ± 0.0244) that scatter tightly around post-baseline mean 2.7053 with no systematic shift. Observational data show 12 new resonator_obs trials (199–204, 336–347 equivalent) that scatter more widely (range 0.1062 cycles/beat vs. lab range 0.0722) and cluster upward. Same-site observational instruments (pendulum_obs and resonator_obs) show opposite drift directions, which is inconsistent with a shared environmental oscillation but consistent with independent observer-specific procedural bias: one observer may round or filter readings differently, apply drift correction inconsistently, or work under fatigue/schedule conditions that introduce systematic bias. Lab observer(s) maintain tight protocol (no within-day level shift, tight scatter). Observational observer operates under decoupled conditions (higher scatter, independent drift direction per instrument). This hypothesis requires verification: checking shift schedules, calibration logs, and reading transcription protocols at both sites. Assigned probability reflects strong internal evidence (bidirectional drift at same site rules out environment, consistent lab protocol argues for observer independence) but requires external documentation to confirm. Downward from p=0.26 because observational drift is now evidently bidirectional *within* the observational site, not just decorrelated from lab; this shifts burden of explanation toward independent instrument drift rather than observer protocol alone.

hypotheses.label: Observational instruments have independent, uncorrelated calibration drift: each instrument drifts on its own timescale, unrelated to shared environment or observer bias
hypotheses.rationale: The observation that pendulum_obs and resonator_obs (co-located at the observational site) show opposite-sign drift on Day 21 (resonator_obs mean +0.0088 above post-baseline, pendulum_obs essentially flat) is the key anomaly. If both instruments were responding to a shared environmental driver (temperature, pressure, humidity oscillation), they should drift *together*, not oppositely. Instead, each instrument appears to have independent drift: resonator_obs drifts upward due to, e.g., optical misalignment specific to that apparatus, while pendulum_obs drifts not at all (or drifts so slowly as to be invisible by Day 21). The lab instruments (pendulum_lab and resonator_lab) show no corresponding drift, which rules out a single environmental mode affecting all four instruments. This hypothesis proposes that each of the four instrument channels has independent instrumental drift with independent timescales and magnitudes—a hypothesis distinct from 'observational observer bias' because it attributes drift to apparatus condition (mechanical creep, thermal drift in sensor electronics, optical degradation) rather than human error. It is also distinct from 'observational calibration chain' (hypothesis 1) because it does not assume a single observational measurement chain but rather four independent channels. This is the most parsimonious explanation for the internal contradiction within the observational site. Probability assigned as: (1) observations support independence (no within-site coherence), (2) but this is a diffuse hypothesis that attributes drift to 'apparatus condition' without specifying mechanism, (3) and requires individual instrument maintenance logs to test. Raised from p=0.10 (where it was bundled into hypothesis 4, 'physical heterogeneity') and separated as its own hypothesis because today's data directly contradicts the 'single shared environmental driver' model.

hypotheses.label: Lag structure (peaks at 2–6 days for same-type pairs, 2–4 days for cross-type pairs) reflects genuine but weak environmental oscillation with ~12–14 day period, damped by site isolation or instrument inertia
hypotheses.rationale: Across all 26 days, same-type instrument pairs show lag peaks at 2–6 days (pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs: r = 0.114 at 4-day lag; resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs: r = 0.198 at 0-day lag), and auto-correlations hint at ~12–14 day oscillation (pendulum_obs 14-day lag: 0.199; resonator_lab 14-day lag: −0.244). However, today's Day 21 data present a critical problem: resonator_obs and pendulum_obs (same site, presumably same environment) show *opposite* drift, not phase-shifted but coherent drift. A genuine shared environmental oscillation would couple both instruments at the same site with the same phase (possibly inverted, but coherent). Instead, we see independent drift directions. This internal contradiction within the observational site is nearly fatal to the 'environmental oscillation' hypothesis. The lag structure could be a coincidental clustering of weak correlations near chance rather than signal. Auto-correlations remain weak and barely above chance (max 0.292). Probability downward from p=0.18 because: (1) same-site opposite drift rules out a single shared environmental mode, (2) auto-correlations are weak and at borderline significance, (3) absence of strong phase coherence within each site argues against periodic forcing. This hypothesis survives only if one imagines highly site-specific resonances (e.g., lab is thermally massive and responds oppositely to a diurnal or 12-day cycle vs. observational site's rapid response), but that moves into the territory of 'physical heterogeneity' (hypothesis 5) with even lower prior.

hypotheses.label: True physical heterogeneity: lab and observational sites couple to genuinely distinct environmental resonances with opposite-phase or site-specific responses
hypotheses.rationale: If the lab site is thermally massive or electromagnetically shielded and the observational site is exposed and responsive to rapid fluctuations, a 12–14 day environmental oscillation could drive opposite-sign responses at the two sites, with 4–6 day lag representing half-period. However, this hypothesis faces a critical obstacle: pendulum_obs and resonator_obs (both at the same observational site) show opposite drift directions on Day 21, not coherent response to the same environment. If both instruments were responding to the same observational site environment, they should respond with the same phase, regardless of opposite-site effects. The internal contradiction within the observational site (same site, opposite drift directions) rules out a simple 'distinct environmental resonances' model that relies on site-level environmental coupling. This hypothesis would require invoking further complexity: instrument-specific resonances within the observational site, or confounding effects that happen to cancel within one instrument but not the other. This is possible but increasingly implausible. Downward from p=0.10 because internal observational-site discord rules out shared environmental driver at that site. This hypothesis now survives only if one proposes that observational instruments have independent mechanical or optical resonances, which moves back toward 'independent instrument drift' (hypothesis 3).

hypotheses.label: Data artifact: computational error in lag-offset search, timestamp misalignment, or transcription error produces spurious correlation structure
hypotheses.rationale: Day 21 measurements (24 new readings across four instruments) confirm that raw data record correctly: no anomalous exact repeats, value spacing consistent (smallest spacing 0.0001 across all instruments), no level shifts. Consistency of lag structure across all four instrument pairs (same-type pairs cluster at short lags, cross-type at longer) is too regular to arise from random computational error. However, absence of validation is concerning: lag-search procedure must be checked against synthetic data with known structure; timestamp alignment must be spot-checked by hand inspection. All correlation values remain weak (max r = 0.406, barely above chance 0.342 for same-type pairs, 0.316 for cross-type), raising concern that noise is being mined for structure. Probability remains very low because structural consistency argues against artifact, but this hypothesis is not closed: validation of lag-search and timestamp alignment is *mandatory* before any publication or decision-making. This is a 'need to verify' not a 'probably true' hypothesis. Assigned p=0.02 as acknowledgment that artifact is unlikely but validation is required.

hypotheses.label: Maintenance, recalibration, or component degradation at observational site occurred between Day 10 and Day 21, causing punctate drift in observational instruments
hypotheses.rationale: If observational equipment underwent service, cleaning, re-zeroing, or component replacement between Day 10 and Day 21, this would explain why observational data show decorrelation from baselines and from lab instruments, with drift accumulating to visible signal level by Day 21. However, today's data do not provide direct evidence of a *punctate* event (step change at a specific day); instead, they show gradual drift or independent instrument-specific bias that may have been present from Day 1 but only reached signal level by Day 21. A maintenance event would show as an abrupt level shift in the affected instrument(s); today's observational data show scatter and gradual drift, not a step. This hypothesis is included because it is the most parsimonious explanation *if* an event occurred, but assigned very low probability pending external verification (observational site maintenance log). Only raise this probability if maintenance log shows an event between Day 10 and Day 21. Assigned p=0.01 as 'need to check external source' rather than 'probable based on data'.

state.question: Why do pendulum_obs and resonator_obs—instruments co-located at the same observational site—exhibit drift in opposite directions (resonator_obs upward, pendulum_obs flat or downward) between Day 10 and Day 30, when a shared environmental driver should couple them coherently; and why do lab and observational instruments remain persistently decorrelated (r < 0.43, near chance) across all 30 days despite identical measurement protocols?

hypotheses.label: Observational site contains two independent instrument-specific calibration drifts, decoupled from each other and from lab measurement chain
hypotheses.rationale: The critical anomaly is that pendulum_obs and resonator_obs, both at the observational site, drift in opposite directions. If they were responding to a shared environmental oscillation or a single observational measurement chain, they should drift together (same phase). Instead, resonator_obs shows post-baseline mean 4.0563 (drift z=+0.32 above baseline 4.0545), while pendulum_obs shows post-baseline mean 2.4991 (drift z=−1.75 below baseline 2.5064). This internal contradiction within a single site is the strongest evidence that each observational instrument has independent calibration drift—likely optical misalignment, thermal sensor drift in resonator electronics, or mechanical creep in pendulum suspension, each operating on its own timescale. Lab instruments (pendulum_lab and resonator_lab) show no corresponding drift (z=−1.35 and z=0.35, both marginal), suggesting either (a) lab calibration is genuinely stable, or (b) any drift is below detection threshold. The persistent decorrelation between lab and observational pairs (pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs r=−0.161 at 3-day lag; resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs r=−0.185 at 1-day lag, both near chance 0.287 and 0.265 respectively) is consistent with independent drift chains: each observational instrument drifts independently, uncoupled from its lab counterpart. Today's measurements (events 457849–439826 for pendulum_lab, 452785–356454 for resonator_lab, 253159–542139 for pendulum_obs, 543609–432838 for resonator_obs) continue to show scatter within expected range; no step-change or sudden recalibration is visible. This supports gradual independent drift rather than a punctate maintenance event. Raised from p=0.19 because opposite-site drift within observational site is now the dominant observed anomaly and this hypothesis directly explains it.

hypotheses.label: Observational measurement team operates under independent calibration schedule or procedural protocol distinct from lab team, introducing systematic observer or transcription bias
hypotheses.rationale: Lab data show tight clustering (e.g., resonator_lab trials 336–347 on Day 21 scatter 0.0722 cycles/beat range around mean 2.7119, tight around baseline 2.7053). Observational data show wider scatter for same instrument type (resonator_obs trials 199–204, 336–347 equivalent show 0.1062 cycles/beat range). If both teams measured the same physical system under identical conditions, they should show similar scatter. The asymmetry (lab tight, observational loose) suggests observational team operates under different conditions: fatigue, outdoor measurement environment (temperature fluctuations, vibration), or decoupled re-zeroing/calibration schedule. However, today's evidence (events 457849–432838) reveals that *within* the observational site, the two instruments drift oppositely, which is harder to explain by observer bias alone—a single observer would apply consistent bias to both instruments. This hypothesis is demoted from p=0.28 because bidirectional within-site drift points toward instrument-specific causes (hypothesis 1) rather than observer protocol. Retained at p=0.24 because observational scatter IS visibly higher than lab scatter, and observer fatigue or procedural inconsistency could amplify pre-existing instrument drifts at the observational site without canceling them. This hypothesis does not explain the opposite-drift pattern but could explain the decorrelation from lab and the higher noise level.

hypotheses.label: Environmental oscillation with ~12–14 day period exists but is so weakly coupled to all four instruments that it remains unresolvable against noise, and internal observational-site opposite drift is unrelated to that oscillation
hypotheses.rationale: Auto-correlations show peaks near 12–14 day lag (pendulum_lab 14-day lag r=0.385, pendulum_obs 14-day lag r=0.229, resonator_lab 13-day lag r=−0.225, resonator_obs 11-day lag r=0.257), and cross-instrument pairs show lag-aligned peaks (pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs r=−0.161 at 3-day offset; resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs r=−0.185 at 1-day offset). These lag structures are statistically weak (mostly at or below chance level for best-match-across-offsets baseline: 0.265–0.296), but their consistency across instrument pairs (same-type pairs cluster at short lags, cross-type at longer) argues against pure artifact. However, the fact that pendulum_obs and resonator_obs drift oppositely within the same site is fatal to a 'single shared environmental driver' hypothesis—they would couple coherently if responding to the same environmental oscillation, even with instrument-specific phase lags. This hypothesis now posits that an environmental oscillation may exist but is weak (~r<0.2) and its effects are drowned out by stronger instrument-specific drifts (hypothesis 1). The opposite-site drift is then unrelated to this oscillation and attributable to independent instrument degradation. This hypothesis is retained at p=0.16 (down from p=0.07) because weak auto-correlations remain consistent with very-low-amplitude periodic forcing, but the internal observational-site contradiction makes it implausible as the primary driver of observed patterns.

hypotheses.label: Observational site underwent maintenance or component degradation between Day 10 and Day 21 that specifically affected resonator_obs (upward drift) and pendulum_obs (downward drift) independently
hypotheses.rationale: If maintenance, cleaning, or re-zeroing occurred at different times for the two observational instruments (or if component degradation progressed at different rates), this could explain opposite-direction drifts. However, today's data show no abrupt level shifts that would signal a punctate maintenance event; instead, scatter and gradual drift are visible. This hypothesis is retained at p=0.10 (down from p=0.01) only as a prompt to check external observational-site maintenance logs. If logs show (a) resonator_obs recalibration or cleaning between Day 10–21, and (b) pendulum_obs re-zeroing or repair at a different time, this hypothesis would rise sharply. Without external documentation, it remains a low-probability placeholder because the *pattern* of opposite drifts is more consistent with independent instrument-specific calibration chains (hypothesis 1) than with a coordinated maintenance event that happened to affect two instruments oppositely.

hypotheses.label: Computational or data-handling error in lag-offset search, timestamp alignment, or transcription has introduced spurious correlation structure that mimics weak periodic signal
hypotheses.rationale: The consistency of lag structure (same-type pairs at short lags, cross-type at longer) across all four instrument pairs is suspicious—it could reflect a systematic bias in the lag-search algorithm rather than genuine signal. However, today's 24 new readings (events 457849–432838) show no anomalous exact repeats, value spacing is consistent (0.0001 minimum across all instruments), and no level shifts appear. This rules out gross transcription errors. Probability remains at p=0.06 (down from p=0.02) because the raw data quality appears sound. However, this hypothesis is not closed: the lag-search procedure must be validated against synthetic data with known structure, and timestamp alignment must be spot-checked by hand before any publication. This is a 'need to verify' not a 'probably false' assessment.

hypotheses.label: Unknown mechanism: something in the interaction between instrument type (pendulum vs. resonator), site location (lab vs. observational), and temporal dynamics that I have not yet formulated
hypotheses.rationale: This residual holds space for mechanisms not yet considered: e.g., if pendulum and resonator instruments respond oppositely to the same hidden driver (e.g., one responds to magnetic field fluctuation, the other to vibration), or if there is a feedback loop between lab and observational measurements that is not apparent from cross-correlations. Kept very low (p=0.02) because the observed anomalies (opposite-site drift within observational site) are already explained by hypothesis 1 (independent instrument drift), which is parsimonious. Residual should rise only if hypothesis 1 fails to account for new observations.

hypotheses.label: Each observational instrument operates on an independent calibration drift timescale, decoupled from its lab counterpart and from the co-located instrument of different type
hypotheses.rationale: The central anomaly is that pendulum_obs and resonator_obs drift oppositely despite co-location. This is inconsistent with any single shared environmental driver or observer bias applied uniformly to both. If they responded to the same external oscillation (thermal, vibration, magnetic), they would couple coherently even with instrument-specific phase lags. Instead, the pattern strongly suggests independent instrument-specific degradation: e.g., pendulum_obs suffers thermal creep in suspension (downward drift), while resonator_obs experiences optical misalignment drift or capacitor drift in resonator electronics (upward drift). Day 40 data show no step-changes or exact repeats (max consecutive repeat run = 1 of 468, matching chance expectation), ruling out sudden maintenance; instead gradual scatter persists, consistent with slow independent degradation. Lab instruments show marginal drift (z≈−1.2 and +0.4, both within ±2), which could reflect genuine stability or drifts below current detection threshold. The persistent decorrelation between lab–obs pairs (pendulum_lab↔pendulum_obs r=0.127 at 2-day lag vs. chance 0.279; resonator_lab↔resonator_obs r=0.171 at 2-day lag vs. chance 0.272) is fully explained by this hypothesis: if each observational instrument drifts independently and lab instruments either remain stable or drift on a different timescale, no coherent coupling between paired instruments would emerge. Raised from p=0.41 because the opposite-drift pattern within a single co-located site is now the most diagnostic feature in the dataset, and this hypothesis directly and parsimoniously explains it without invoking external events or procedural changes.

hypotheses.label: Observational measurement team operates under different environmental conditions or calibration discipline than lab team, amplifying instrument-specific drifts without creating them
hypotheses.rationale: Observational data show higher scatter than lab data for same instrument type (e.g., resonator_obs trials 199–204 span 0.1062 cycles/beat; comparable lab trials span tighter range). This is consistent with outdoor or less-controlled measurement environment (temperature swings, vibration, humidity), or observational team's independent re-zeroing schedule or fatigue effects. However, this hypothesis does not explain why observational instruments drift *oppositely*—a single environmental perturbation (temperature, vibration) would bias both instruments in the same direction, or at least not produce sustained opposite drifts. This hypothesis is retained because it explains the *magnitude* of observational scatter and the decorrelation from lab, but demoted from p=0.24 because it does not address the core anomaly (opposite drifts). It now serves as a secondary explanation for *why* observational drifts are larger in absolute magnitude than lab drifts, not for why they differ in sign. hypotheses.label: Weak environmental oscillation (~12–14 day period) exists but is so small in amplitude that it remains unresolvable against noise and is not the driver of the opposite-drift pattern

This hypothesis is therefore reframed: an environmental oscillation may exist, but it is weaker than or orthogonal to the instrument-specific drifts (hypothesis 1) and does not explain the core anomaly. The weak auto-correlations are retained as a 'need to follow up' rather than a leading hypothesis.
